title: Lesson 5. Positioning
description: static, relative, absolute, fixed and sticky

learn.intro: Hi! Lesson 5 — **positioning**. We'll learn to pull an element out of the «queue» and put it where we want — for example, a red SALE badge in the corner of a picture. Let's go!

slides.text: Imagine a queue in a shop: everyone stands one after another, nobody can step ahead. That's how elements stand on a site by default. It's called **normal flow**.
`position: static` is the **default** state. If you write nothing, an element is static: an ordinary queue, nothing moves. You can see it in DevTools.
If position isn't set — it's static.

check.prompt: What position does an element have if you write nothing?

slides.text: We move the box 20px down and to the right:
The box moved, but it **didn't leave its place in the queue**. The neighbors stayed where they were, as if it weren't there.
Try to guess: where will the block go with `top: -20px`? Right — **up**.

check.prompt: With position: relative the neighbors move along with the element.
check.explain: The element moves, but its place in the flow remains — the neighbors stay put.

check.prompt: Where will the block move with top: -20px?
check.explain: A negative top lifts the block up.

slides.text: `absolute` means a person **leaves the queue completely**, and the others ignore them. They look for the **nearest parent with relative** to attach to. If there's none, they attach to the whole page.
The bug: the badge flew to the corner of the **whole page** because the card has no relative. It found only body:
We fix it — give the parent `position: relative`. Now the badge is «caught» inside the card and moves with it:
absolute always looks for the nearest relative ancestor. If it doesn't find one, it flies off to body.

check.prompt: An absolute badge flew to the corner of the page. What do you fix?
check.explain: absolute attaches to the nearest relative parent.

check.prompt: An absolute element stays in the queue and pushes its neighbors.
check.explain: absolute leaves the flow — the neighbors don't notice it.

slides.text: `fixed` means the element is **nailed to the screen**. You scroll the page, and it stays in place. That's how «back to top» buttons and online-shop panels work.
A «back to top» button in the bottom-right corner of the screen:

check.prompt: What happens to a fixed button when you scroll the page?
options: It stays in place on the screen
It scrolls away with the page
check.explain: fixed is attached to the screen, not the page.

slides.text: `sticky` is a clever hybrid. Until you reach a certain point, it behaves like **static**. Once you scroll there, it **sticks**, like fixed.
The header sticks to the top while scrolling:
Without top: 0, sticky won't work — it needs a sticking point. Also check that the parent has no overflow: hidden.

check.prompt: If you remove top: 0, sticky still sticks.
check.explain: sticky needs a sticking point, such as top: 0.

sections.title: Practice: a SALE badge and homework

slides.text: Task: a product card with a red «SALE» badge in the top-right corner. First give the parent `position: relative` — that's your «anchor». Then give the badge `position: absolute`, `top` and `right`.
Bonus: 3 cards with «-12%», «NEW» and «HIT» badges. Whoever is fastest earns the title of **positioning master** 🏅
Homework: a site header with `position: sticky` that sticks to the top. Take 20–30 paragraphs of text so the page is long.
relative shifts, absolute pulls out of the queue and attaches to a relative parent, fixed nails to the screen, and sticky sticks once you scroll to its point.

check.prompt: Match the position and what it does

questions.prompt: By default every element has position: static.
What's the ordinary order called, where elements stand one after another?
questions.explain: Normal flow — like a queue in a shop.

options: Move the box 20px down and to the right
Move the box up and to the left
Nail the box to the screen
Take the box out of the flow
questions.explain: top: 20px goes down from the top, left: 20px goes right from the left edge.

questions.prompt: An element with relative keeps its place in the queue.
questions.explain: The neighbors stay put as if it hadn't moved.

questions.prompt: Which top value lifts a relative block 20px up? (with px)
questions.explain: A negative value moves it the other way.

questions.prompt: What does an element with position: absolute attach to?
questions.explain: With no relative parent, it attaches to body.

questions.prompt: Where will the badge end up?
options: In the corner of the whole page
In the corner of the card
questions.explain: There's no relative parent — the badge attached to body.

questions.prompt: Build the rule that makes the card an «anchor» for the badge
If the parent gets position: relative, an absolute badge moves together with the card.
questions.explain: The badge is attached to the card, not lying on the screen.

questions.prompt: Which position suits a «back to top» button that's always visible in the screen corner?
questions.explain: fixed is nailed to the screen and doesn't scroll away.

options: In the bottom-right corner of the screen
In the top-left corner of the page
At the end of the page, after the text
questions.explain: bottom and right are measured from the edges of the screen.

questions.prompt: How does sticky behave before you scroll to its point?
options: Like fixed — nailed to the screen
Like absolute — out of the flow

questions.prompt: A sticky header doesn't stick. What do you check?
options: There's no top: 0 — it needs a sticking point
questions.explain: sticky only works with a sticking point, such as top: 0.

questions.prompt: Match the position and an example on a site
pairs: A SALE badge in a card corner
A header that sticks to the top

questions.prompt: SALE badge: what do you give the card and the badge?
options: relative to the card, absolute to the badge
absolute to the card, relative to the badge
questions.explain: The parent is the «anchor» (relative), the badge attaches to it (absolute).
